prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states that founded the field of moire quantum matter

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is the candidate on which the committee is most broadly united: six of eight members place it in their top three even though only one puts it first, so it is the widest common ground rather than a narrow enthusiasm. The 2011 Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum-model calculation is a genuine electronic-structure prediction: a quantitative statement that a purely geometric parameter, the twist angle, quenches the Dirac velocity and produces nearly flat bands, made before any experiment and from a model whose ingredients (interlayer tunnelling, band folding) are standard in my own field. The 2018 discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity by the Jarillo-Herrero group then showed that a clean carbon system can host strongly correlated physics, which few of us expected. In my 2025 remarks I said that quantum mechanics continually offers new surprises; this is a surprise of exactly that kind, and it has since propagated to fractional Chern insulators, moire transition-metal dichalcogenides and a large independent literature. The theory-plus-experiment structure is clean and the three names define a coherent prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity and attribution. The microscopic origin of the superconductivity is still debated, sample-to-sample variation and twist-angle disorder complicate several phases, and a committee that prefers settled interpretations could reasonably say it is early. On attribution, the first experimental author (Yuan Cao) and other groups (Dean, Young, Yazdani) contributed decisively to the experimental programme and are outside the three-person limit, and the theory credit cannot be fully separated from earlier twist-angle band-structure work by others (for example Lopes dos Santos and collaborators). Compared with B058 or B024, which are mature and more cleanly attributed, B003 is the riskier and more contested choice.

responses.point: Johansson ranks optical lattice clocks (B024) first, arguing that the two-person credit is clean, that the work has been confirmed independently by many laboratories for more than a decade and that it is a natural successor to the 2005 frequency-comb prize. He ranks circuit QED second but discloses ties to Chalmers and WACQT and notes the timing problem after the 2025 circuit prize.
responses.response: I agree with most of this and regard B024 as the best-attributed and most mature candidate on the list; that is why it is my first alternative. Where I differ is in weighting. Clock accuracy at the 10^-18 level is a superb measurement achievement, but I am judging it outside my specialty, on clarity and impact, and the new-phase-of-matter character of the moire discovery seems to me to carry more physics content than an improvement in precision, however spectacular. I also welcome Johansson's open disclosure on circuit QED, and I share his view that a second circuit-based prize one year after 2025 is hard to justify, so I do not push B043.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics (B001) first on the grounds that its impact is routine and field-wide, that the Rose-Haider-Urban chain maps naturally onto a three-person prize and that recognition is overdue. She ranks twisted bilayer graphene second but would credit only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero.
responses.response: I take the instrumentation case seriously, because I ranked a computational method first myself and cannot consistently dismiss tool-building. The disagreement is one of degree: B001 has strong attribution, but it appears on only one opening ballot, so it has no visible path to a majority. On B003, I accept that MacDonald is the principal voice on the theory side and that a two-name version is defensible, but I would keep Bistritzer, since the 2011 paper is a two-author calculation and dropping its first author is hard to justify. If the committee prefers two names it should say explicitly why.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks active matter and flocking (B006) first as a conceptually original statistical-physics result, with Toner-Tu theory and the Vicsek transition forming a fair trio, while noting that quantitative verification of the Toner-Tu exponents is incomplete. He places Car-Parrinello sixth as a methodological invention that may be seen as more chemistry than physics.
responses.response: I accept his caution about the exponents, but the qualitative result, long-range order in two dimensions in a non-equilibrium system, is real physics and I would not dismiss it. We differ over B058. I understand the worry that Car-Parrinello is a method, but it changed what questions can be asked about liquids, defects and reactions, and Kohn's 1998 chemistry prize recognized the density functional, not the dynamics. Since I rank B058 first myself, I must be open about the possible bias of a computational materials theorist, and I do not consider that a good basis for a proposal that has so little support. I therefore keep it as an alternative and not as my preferred configuration.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks magic-angle graphene first as a clear, original discovery of new phases, confirmed by many groups and now ripe, but flags that the first-author experimentalist is omitted and that the superconducting mechanism is unsettled. He ranks topological insulators (B023) second.
responses.response: I agree that the timing is ripe and that an unsettled pairing mechanism should not block a prize for the discovery of the phases themselves. I share his worry about the omitted experimentalist, but the three-person rule forces that cost and I see no way among the supplied names to remove it. On B023, which I rank second, I think it is the best fallback if B003 stalls, but with the 2016 prize on topological phases the novelty argument is weaker than for moire matter, and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the three-dimensional materials complicate the three names.

responses.point: Pearce ranks optical lattice clocks first as an original, clean and experimentally decisive invention, timely and arguably overdue, and ranks twisted bilayer graphene second, while noting that overlap with the frequency-comb and ion-clock prizes may be raised.
responses.response: Pearce and I both place B003 and B024 in our top four and differ mainly in order, so this is the most useful comparison on the table. His point about overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is fair but I think manageable: the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct idea from the comb and from single-ion control. What tips my order is that B024 has very clean attribution and maturity, while B003 offers more new physics. I would accept B024 as the committee's choice if the discussion shows that the interpretation of the moire superconductivity is judged too unsettled, and I would like colleagues to say what degree of interpretive maturity they require.

uncertainties: Whether the unresolved pairing mechanism and the dependence on twist-angle disorder make B003 premature relative to B024.
Whether the committee would accept two names (MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero) or must name Bistritzer, and how to treat the uncredited first experimental author within the three-person limit.
Whether a computational method such as Car-Parrinello (B058) can be weighed as a physics discovery, given that only two members ranked it.
Overlap of B024 with the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and of B023 with the 2016 topological-phase prize.
I rely on recollection of dates and priority and have not verified them against external sources.
statement.conflict_note: No specific personal or institutional conflict with the credited names of B003, B024 or B058 is apparent from my provided profile. I work in electronic-structure theory and magnetism, so I have field proximity to B058 and B023 and formed my opening ranking from that perspective; I flag this as a possible bias, not as a documented connection.
